title: Drop-stitch scarf
subtitle: Deliberately dropped stitches create open columns in a lightweight scarf.
excerpt: A flat scarf worked in garter stitch with periodic yarn-overs that are dropped on the following row to create open, elongated columns, knitted on 5 mm needles with DK yarn. Finished dimensions are 22 cm wide by 175 cm long.
sourceNotes: Drop-stitch patterns using deliberate yarn-overs that are subsequently dropped appear in Victorian lace manuals as a simplified openwork technique. The elongated-loop pattern is described in Weldon's Practical Knitter under simplified lace grounds. Adapts these principles for a modern lightweight scarf format.
heroPrompt: A drop-stitch scarf in pale silver DK yarn showing the open elongated columns against the garter-stitch background, laid flat on a light surface to show the openwork texture.

glossaryTerms.definition: Wrapping the yarn over the needle before the next stitch to create a new loop. In a drop-stitch pattern, these extra loops are deliberately dropped off the needle on the following row to form elongated open columns.

A knitting technique where stitches or yarn-overs are deliberately allowed to fall off the needle and unravel to a controlled depth, creating open columns in the fabric. The dropped loops elongate the adjacent stitches and create an airy openwork effect.
A cast-on using the tail and working yarn together to form an elastic, neat edge.

content.text: This is a flat scarf worked on 5 mm needles with DK yarn, finishing at 22 cm wide and 175 cm long. Garter stitch forms the base; periodic yarn-overs are dropped on the next row to open up columns of
drop stitches
across the body. The result is lighter and more open than plain garter without needing a chart.

Flat construction was chosen because the drop-stitch pattern is worked in rows, and the yarn-overs that create the open columns are placed and dropped across a flat surface. The technique is simpler than lace: you add
yarn overs
on Row 3 and deliberately let them slide off the needle on Row 4, elongating the stitches below them. The scarf uses about 175 g (395 m / 432 yards) of DK yarn.
What you need

items.name: DK-weight wool or cotton yarn
items.substitutions: A smooth yarn shows the drop-stitch columns most clearly. Avoid heavily textured or hairy yarns that cling.

items.name: 5 mm needles (UK 6 / US 8)
items.substitutions: The slightly large needle size creates more open garter ridges.

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 30 rows = 10 x 10 cm in garter stitch on 5 mm needles. The drop-stitch sections open up and the finished scarf measures approximately 22 cm wide. If your gauge reads tighter than 18 sts per 10 cm, the scarf will be narrower; if looser, the open columns will be more pronounced and the scarf wider.
Stitches used
K (knit), YO (yarn over). The YOs added on Row 3 are dropped off the needle on Row 4 as you pass each stitch.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on
to place 40 stitches. Tail length: (15.7 x 40) / 10 + 15 = about 78 cm.
Stitch count check-in: 40 stitches after the cast-on.
Body
Rows 1 and 2: K to end. (40 sts)
Row 3 (YO row): (K1, YO) to end, K0. You will have 80 stitches on the needle after this row. This is correct.
Row 4 (drop row): K across, dropping each YO off the needle as you reach it. Do not knit the YOs; slip them off. You will return to 40 stitches. (40 sts)
Stitch count check-in: after Row 4, count the stitches: back to 40. The dropped YOs elongate the stitches below them to form the open columns.
Repeat the four-row pattern until the scarf measures 175 cm from the cast-on edge. At the halfway mark (about 87 cm), after a drop row, confirm: still 40 stitches.
Cast off
Cast off after a Row 2 (plain garter row). Work the standard cast-off knitting each stitch and passing the previous one over. Work loosely.
Common faults

Knitting the YOs instead of dropping them. If you knit the YOs on the drop row, the fabric will have double the stitch count and will narrow and thicken noticeably. When you reach a YO loop on the drop row, slip it off the left needle with a flick of the needle tip without knitting it.
Open columns that are too narrow. This happens when the YO row is worked too tightly. Work Row 3 loosely, exaggerating the size of each yarn-over.
Uneven column spacing. On Row 3 the instruction is YO after every knit stitch, maintaining a consistent spacing of one YO per stitch. Counting stitches before and after Row 3 catches missed YOs.
Finishing
Weave in ends. The open columns relax after washing. A gentle wet block pins the scarf to its final width and allows the drop columns to open fully.
Care
Handwash wool in cool water, press out moisture gently, and lay flat to dry. The open columns may close slightly in the wash and open again as the scarf dries.
What to try next
The eyelet lace scarf uses yarn-overs paired with decreases to create a fully patterned lace fabric. Or try the fringed garter scarf for a classic lightweight finish.
